title: Justified by faith (Romans 3:21–28)
hookLine: Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification in 1999, after centuries of argument
carry: all have sinned, all are loved

lines: FIVE CENTURIES OVER A FEW VERSES.
cards: October thirty-first, 1999. Augsburg, Germany. The Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation sign the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification.
The date is deliberate: Lutherans keep October thirty-first as the anniversary of the start of the Reformation. So is the city: Augsburg is where Lutherans set out their beliefs in 1530.
For almost five centuries, this one question had divided Western Christians. At its root lay a few verses of Romans.

teach.b: Justification translates a Greek word family built on dikaios, righteous: being made right, or set right, with God.
In Romans 3, Paul has just spent two chapters showing that no one, Jew or Gentile, stands right with God by their own record.
Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God." All. No exceptions, no ranking of who's worse.
And in the next breath: being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. All have sinned, and all are offered grace as a gift.
A few verses later: "For we account a man to be justified by faith, without the works of the law."
When Martin Luther translated that verse into German, he added a word: allein, alone. Justified by faith alone. That word became a battle line.
Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith, not by anything they earn.
The Council of Trent, for Catholics, stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous within, and that faith works through love. Each side heard the other as denying something essential.
The 1999 declaration didn't erase every difference.

But both churches stated together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work, and not because of any merit of ours, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works.
They said the old condemnations no longer apply to the teaching as each side now explains it. Later, Methodists, Reformed and Anglican churches joined or welcomed it.

how: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is God's free gift received in baptism, which both forgives sin and renews the person within; it joined the Lutheran World Federation in the 1999 Joint Declaration, and many local parishes pray with Lutheran neighbors during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

a legal excuse that clears someone's record

p: grace truly makes a person righteous

s: the 1999 declaration ended every difference between the churches
it stated a shared understanding of the basics and lifted old condemnations, but differences remain.
Luther added the word alone to Romans 3:28 in German
allein. it became a battle line for centuries.

games.q: you're part of a dialogue between two churches that have condemned each other's teaching for centuries. what do you aim for?
o: get the other side to admit it was wrong.
find what both can say together, and name what's still different.
agree to stop talking about it.
games.why: the joint declaration states a shared understanding of grace and faith, says the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as now explained, and is honest that differences remain.

practice: Hold in mind a Lutheran church you drive past, or a Lutheran friend, coworker or in-law.
Remember that for centuries both sides were taught to see each other as wrong about the most important thing, and that at Augsburg both signed the same words about grace.
If you pray, ask blessing on them by name; if not, just wish them well, sincerely.

wordCard.voice: Justification. Being set right with God, freely, by grace: the word that divided Catholics and Lutherans for centuries, and that they spoke together in 1999. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: righteousness, justice, being right with God. justification comes from the same family.

carryVoice: Your line: all have sinned, all are loved. The word all leaves no one out. That's day five hundred sixty-one.
